demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma involving unexpected death of a loved one, repeated triggers centered on children (kids crying, being around children) are hard to explain unless the deceased was a child or the death specifically involved children; with no supporting memory, threat, or appraisal content linking the loss to children, this trigger pattern is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Avoiding sex is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The reported triggers and appraisals focus on grief/disconnection rather than bodily violation, intimacy threat, or sexual trauma themes, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the selected items.

Feeling 'like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal violation, coercion, or depersonalized trauma responses. In a bereavement profile, without corroborating memory, trigger, or strategy content suggesting objectification or dissociation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For traumatic bereavement, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. There are no memory, threat, or appraisal items linking the loss to children or parenting, so this trigger feels clinically unanchored relative to the rest of the profile.

'Avoid Sex' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the self-report. Sexual avoidance is more typically anchored to interpersonal/sexual trauma or marked contamination/intimacy themes, none of which are represented elsewhere in the selected triggers or appraisals for a bereavement presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is poorly matched to unexpected death of a loved one in the absence of other humiliation, assault, or depersonalization-related content. It does not cohere well with the grief-linked triggers and appears disconnected from the stated maladaptive strategies and formulation.

vignette:
María is a 38-year-old Latina woman who works on an assembly line at a food-processing plant, a job she has held for over a decade. Two years ago, her younger brother, Carlos, died unexpectedly from a sudden cardiac arrest at the age of 34. He collapsed at home, and by the time the paramedics arrived, it was too late. María was the one who called 911, and she held his hand as the sirens wailed closer, certain they would save him. They did not. In the weeks that followed, she found herself unable to attend his funeral—the thought of standing near a grave made her feel as though the earth itself might swallow her—and she began avoiding any conversation where someone mentioned losing a loved one, because the words hit her like a physical blow.

At work, the plant is near a fire station, and sirens pass by several times a day. Each time one sounds, María’s chest tightens, and she feels the heat of that afternoon crawl up her throat. She has come to believe that her life has been destroyed by the trauma, that she used to be a happy person but is now always miserable, and that she no longer belongs anywhere—not even in her own family, who she feels have moved on without her. When the sirens wail, these thoughts surge forward with fresh force: she is certain that her happiness is gone forever, that she is a ghost in her own life. She now finds herself scanning the factory floor for any reminder of loss—a coworker’s black dress, a condolence card pinned to a bulletin board—and each sighting reinforces her sense that she is fundamentally broken and isolated from the world.

To manage this, María has developed a pattern of going over and over the details of Carlos’s death, replaying the phone call, the ambulance, the hospital room, trying to make sense of why it happened, as if she might find a hidden explanation that would undo it. She also keeps asking her sister—the only person she still talks to about it—whether she is okay, whether she seems normal, whether people can tell something is wrong with her. The reassurance never lasts. Each time she hung up the phone, the very fact that she had needed to ask felt like proof that something was deeply wrong with her, confirming her belief that she was no longer the person she used to be. After a long shift where she has been triggered by a siren or a stray comment about loss, she will call her sister late at night, and the conversation will leave her feeling emptier, more convinced that her life has no purpose left. The overanalyzing itself deepens her sense of misery, because the more she turns the event over in her mind, the more she feels like a stranger to herself, someone who cannot move forward.

Over the past year, María has stopped visiting her mother’s house entirely, because her mother keeps a photo of Carlos on the mantel and a framed Mass card on the refrigerator. She has also stopped going to the grocery store near the cemetery, taking a longer bus route instead, and she no longer answers calls from friends who she fears might bring up grief. At work, she has asked to be moved to a quieter part of the line, away from the loading dock where the sirens are loudest, and her supervisor has accommodated her, but she knows her coworkers have noticed. One of them asked her last month if she was okay, and she snapped at them, then spent the rest of the shift ruminating about whether she had ruined the relationship. She is certain that people see her as damaged, and this belief makes her hypervigilant to any sign of pity or distance from others, which in turn sends her back into the spiral of replaying the trauma.

What finally brought María to seek help was a moment last week when a siren passed during her lunch break and she dropped her sandwich, unable to breathe, and a coworker had to guide her to a chair. That night, she realized she could not keep living this way—she was afraid she would lose her job, or worse, that she would stop caring entirely. She hopes therapy can give her a way to stop the endless replaying of that afternoon, and she is terrified that nothing will ever make her feel like she belongs in the world again.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that María's maladaptive strategies (rumination, reassurance seeking) cause or lead to her negative appraisals; the text shows they deepen her misery but does not link them as a cause of the appraisals themselves.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that María's maladaptive strategies (rumination, reassurance seeking) cause or lead to her negative appraisals; the text shows they deepen her misery but does not link them as a cause of the appraisals themselves.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
